title: HKMA’s ART Framework Puts Bank AI Governance in Focus
excerpt: . Back to News / Technology. Build your reading streak 0 / 3 today · Counts at 25%. On 15 October, Hong Kong’s banking regulator issued updated supervisory guidance for responsible AI use, putting accountability, resilience and trust at the centre of how banks govern systems that can plan and act across multiple steps. The package is called ART, but it is not a new statute. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s circular is addressed to all authorized institutions and calls for timely updates to policies, procedures and controls. Its accompanying guidance replaces the HKMA’s 2019 high-level AI principles and asks institutions to apply expectations proportionately to their use of AI and associated risks. Status is uneven: guidance is issued; second-cohort trials are complete; the platform is planned; and further agent testing and a governance discussion paper remain ahead. Board ownership and risk-based controls. The new guidance treats AI as an institution-wide governance issue rather than a software purchase. Boards should approve an AI strategy and risk appetite, while senior management maintains oversight. Institutions remain responsible for AI-generated outcomes, including when a third-party provider supplies the system. The practical expectations include:. A named owner for each AI use case already deployed, with authority to oversee controls and escalate problems. An up-to-date inventory of approved uses, including internally built, third-party and embedded AI, with each case’s purpose, provider, model, risk classification and key controls. Risk-proportionate checks throughout the lifecycle: testing and validation before deployment or material changes, ongoing monitoring, fallback and recovery plans, and auditable records. The guidance also covers data governance, privacy, vendor dependencies, cybersecurity, explainability and fair treatment of customers. For material or higher-risk applications, it calls for more stringent review and, where appropriate, independent validation or adversarial testing. It says human oversight can range from “human-in-the-loop” review to “human-on-the-loop” monitoring or “human-in-command”, depending on the use case. A reviewer must have the competence, information, time and authority to challenge or stop the system. This is not a blanket mandate for real-time human approval of every AI output. The circular calls for proportionate application and asks institutions to use existing governance where appropriate. Sandbox figures describe trials, not rollout. The updated expectations draw on the second cohort of the HKMA’s Generative AI Sandbox. Announced in October 2025, that cohort selected 27 use cases involving 20 banks and 14 technology partners from more than 60 proposals. The HKMA said technical trials concluded on 15 October 2026. More than 60% of the use cases explored agentic AI; that is a share of use cases, not of banks, and does not mean those systems are operating across the banking sector. In remarks the next day, HKMA banking supervisor Carmen Chu said half of the agent-related use cases involved multiple agents. The authority also cited examples from the trials: a bank’s fraud-detection work was associated with a 40% reduction in customer-onboarding time; a wealth-management chatbot recorded 98% positive feedback; and one market-risk agent shortened a case-analysis cycle by 95%. These are regulator-reported, case-specific results. The public remarks do not identify an independent audit, common measurement method or evidence that the results transfer to other banks. RTHK separately reported that Standard Chartered trialled a client-information summariser and HSBC a deepfake detector. It relayed Standard Chartered’s estimate that one task dropped from four to five hours to about a minute. The Gold. ADVANCED. Published: 18:08, October 15, 2026 | Updated: 08:57, October 16, 2026. HKMA launches framework for responsible AI adoption in banking. By Yancy Fang in Hong Kong. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on Thursday unveiled a framework to support the responsible adoption of artificial intelligence by the local banking sector while maintaining robust governance and operational resilience. Designed under HKMA's Fintech 2030 strategy, the "ART" Framework stands for “Accountability”, “Resilience” and “Trust”. It aims to provide a clear foundation for banks to develop and deploy AI responsibly, fostering an AI-enabled banking ecosystem. READ MORE: iAM Smart AI assistant to answer queries on HK govt services. The move to support banks in seizing the opportunities presented by AI comes with AI systems becoming more autonomous, with greater access to data, tools and workflows. “The progression from generative to agentic AI represents an important new stage of innovation for the banking sector,” said Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, deputy chief executive of the HKMA. By pairing innovation with clear accountability, resilient operating models and effective human oversight, banks can fully realize the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust and stability for Hong Kong's financial system, Yuen added. The key initiatives under the "ART" Framework include Supervisory Guidance for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence, drawing on insights from the second cohort of the Generative AI (GenAI) Sandbox and an AI training data sharing platform in collaboration with Hong Kong Cyberport Management Company Ltd and The University of Hong Kong, with data quality assurance as a core design principle. Sandbox++ and an upcoming discussion paper on a proposed supervisory framework for agentic A. I. governance, exploring intent-anchored accountability, a registry of material AI agents and effective intervention mechanisms, according to the HKMA statement. To mark the successful completion of the technical trials under the second cohort of the GenAI Sandbox, the HKMA is also co-hosting the two-day Finance+A. I. Forum with Cyberport on Thursday and Friday. More than 60 percent of the use cases explored agentic AI, demonstrating the industry's active pursuit of advanced AI applications, such as automated planning and execution of multi-step tasks within defined boundaries and controls, the statement added.
